services.name: OpenAI API
services.description: OpenAI's managed API platform for its text, reasoning, image, audio, realtime, embedding, moderation, and related model families.
services.service_boundary: Represents the developer API platform, not ChatGPT, Codex, individual model releases, or Azure-hosted OpenAI models.
services.regional_controls: Eligible API organizations can configure project-level regional storage and, for supported regions, regional processing; eligibility and endpoint coverage vary.
services.retention_controls: API data is not used for model training unless the customer opts in. Default abuse-monitoring and application-state retention vary by endpoint; approved organizations can use Modified Abuse Monitoring or Zero Data Retention with documented feature limitations.
services.routing: Customers select models within OpenAI's catalog; the service is not a cross-provider routing layer.
services.customization: Fine-tuning and stored application resources are available for eligible models and endpoints, with separate retention behavior.
strengths: One first-party platform spans multiple modalities, realtime interaction, tools, batch processing, and model customization.
Project-level administration, data controls, and regional endpoints are documented in the API platform.
tradeoffs: Regional processing, Zero Data Retention, and some enterprise controls require eligibility and do not cover every endpoint or feature.
The service exposes OpenAI models rather than a vendor-neutral catalog.

findings.claim: We detect global cache sharing across users in seven API providers, including OpenAI, resulting in potential privacy leakage about users' prompts. The paper reports the OpenAI issue was patched after responsible disclosure before publication; its first version is dated 2025-02-11.

resolved.summary: The current prompt-caching guide states that caches are not shared across organizations, and the paper reports the issue was patched after disclosure.

services.name: OpenRouter
services.description: A unified API and billing layer that routes model requests across multiple upstream inference providers and model publishers.
services.service_boundary: Represents OpenRouter's API routing service, not the upstream providers, the underlying model releases, or OpenRouter's end-user chat interface.
services.regional_controls: Enterprise customers can use documented EU in-region routing; provider and endpoint selection otherwise determines where upstream processing occurs.
services.retention_controls: OpenRouter documents opt-in prompt logging and per-request controls that restrict routing by upstream retention or data-collection policy; upstream provider behavior remains part of the effective boundary.
services.routing: Requests can use ordered providers, fallbacks, allowlists, denylists, privacy requirements, price ceilings, and latency or throughput preferences.
services.customization: The public service focuses on routing existing models and provider endpoints; private customer endpoints are documented separately as an enterprise beta and are not treated as a stable catalog capability here.
strengths: A single compatible API can express fallback, cost, latency, throughput, and data-policy constraints across providers.
Endpoint-level retention metadata makes privacy part of routing rather than a provider-wide assumption.
tradeoffs: Requests cross an additional service boundary before reaching an upstream inference provider.
Effective terms, availability, and data handling depend on both OpenRouter and the selected upstream endpoint.

Two 2026 measurement studies report cross-account prompt-cache reads at upstream providers for traffic on OpenRouter's shared credentials; the operator documents no cache scope for that path, and bring-your-own-key routes were isolated where tested.

findings.claim: OpenRouter's use of shared organizational credentials enables cross-account cache sharing that would not occur when accessing providers directly. Tested against three upstream providers with one model each; isolation held when the same providers were reached directly or through OpenRouter's bring-your-own-key mode.

source.label: CacheProbe: Auditing Prompt Cache Isolation in Gateway APIs, arXiv 2605.30613v1

findings.claim: Large language model (LLM) API relays authenticate customers separately but often forward requests through shared provider credentials. In an outcome-independent weekly OpenRouter frame, tests covered 80.5% of eligible token volume and found cross-account reads for 12 of 28 labels carrying 33.7% of volume.

source.label: KeyPooling: Measuring Where LLM API Relay Paths Collapse Prompt Cache Isolation, arXiv 2608.17485v1

It is not the Laguna weight releases, not self-managed Poolside inference that customers deploy on their own Kubernetes or on-premises hardware, not the Poolside Agent CLI or Poolside Assistant clients, and not Poolside models served by OpenRouter or other third parties.
services.regional_controls: The documentation exposes one global base URL and establishes no customer-selected processing region, regional endpoint, private networking, or dedicated placement. Customers who need to control placement are directed to a self-managed Poolside inference deployment on their own AWS EKS, OpenShift, upstream Kubernetes, or on-premises hardware, which is a customer-operated execution path rather than a mode of this service.
services.retention_controls: The Poolside Terms of Use permit using Content, defined to include prompts, code, and output, to provide and improve the Products and to train Poolside models unless the user opts out. The opt-out is described as a Training Opt-Out setting for access through the Site, with third-party platforms governed by their own controls, and it does not apply to Content submitted as feedback or flagged for safety review. A Data Processing Addendum and a privacy policy are published; no zero-retention mode, per-request retention control, or customer deletion path is documented for the hosted API.
services.routing: Callers name a published Poolside model id such as poolside/laguna-s-2.1. The service serves only Poolside's own models and documents no cross-provider routing, fallback, replica steering, or priority tier.
services.customization: No fine-tuning, adapter training, customer-supplied weights, or dedicated deployment is documented for the hosted API. Control is per request through the OpenAI-compatible parameters and a thinking toggle, and per model through published model ids; larger context windows are directed to paid access through OpenRouter rather than a tier of this service.
strengths: A direct first-party path to Poolside's own coding models over ordinary OpenAI-compatible chat completions, usable from any OpenAI SDK with only a base URL and key change.

Support is documented rather than implied: two published tiers with first-response time targets, a support portal with a defined scope that names inference availability and error rates, and dated model and inference release notes.
tradeoffs: Training on customer prompts, code, and output is the documented default, and the opt-out is an account setting rather than a per-request or per-key control.

The surface is narrow: one global endpoint pair, on-demand only, no documented regions, fallback, batch, reserved capacity, or fine-tuning, with larger context windows pointed at a third-party router.

services.name: Sakana Fugu
services.description: A Japanese lab's API serving its own model identities, where the flagship is a multi-agent system that orchestrates an undisclosed pool of frontier models behind a single model name.
services.service_boundary: Represents the operator's public API platform at api.sakana.ai and the model identities it exposes, not the orchestrated third-party models inside the pool, the lab's separate consumer chat, translation, and analyst products, or its published research code.
services.regional_controls: No customer-selectable processing region is exposed. The service is not offered in the European Union or European Economic Area, which the product page attributes to pending GDPR compliance work, and the terms extend that exclusion and reserve the right to enforce it by technical means including IP address controls. The privacy policy states that personal data may be transferred outside the user's country of residence, naming Japan and the United States, and describes recipients only as categories of vendors without naming a sub-processor.
services.retention_controls: The terms state that the operator is not obligated to retain or store prompts, files, or other submitted data, placing the backup burden on the customer, and permit deletion with or without prior notice. Training use is the default rather than an exception: the operator reserves the right to use customer content to train, retrain, and fine-tune its own models. An opt-out is available through the service interface, but the terms state that the effects of prior training use may not be reversible retroactively and that content may still be used to provide the service, comply with law, and maintain security. No zero-retention tier, data-processing agreement, or audit attestation is published.
services.routing: Routing is the product rather than a caller-facing control. The flagship identity dispatches each request across an internal pool of frontier models and returns a single response; the operator states that the pool's membership is proprietary and not exposed by design. The base tier lets a customer exclude specific models from its pool through the console for data, privacy, or compliance reasons, while the top tier's pool is fixed because it depends on the full set. No fallback, regional steering, replica, or failover behavior is documented.
services.customization: No fine-tuning, adapter training, or customer-weight deployment is documented. Customization is limited to choosing among the published model identities, pinning a versioned alias of the top tier, and excluding models from the base tier's pool. A separate Japanese-focused model identity with built-in web search and code execution is offered under the same key.
strengths: Three request contracts — OpenAI chat completions, OpenAI responses, and Anthropic messages — share one base URL and one console-issued key.
Pool exclusion is an operational privacy control rather than a promise: a customer with a vendor restriction can remove that vendor from the base tier's pool themselves.
Both governing documents are current and dated, and the top tier publishes pinned version aliases alongside the moving one.
tradeoffs: Training on customer content is the default posture, and the opt-out is explicitly not retroactive.
The orchestrated pool is undisclosed by design, so a caller cannot establish which third party processed a given request or under whose terms.

One synchronous on-demand path with no batch, reserved capacity, dedicated endpoint, regional endpoint, or documented failover, and no published service-level agreement, data-processing agreement, sub-processor list, or third-party audit.
